L27: # Qualified majority
L28: 
L29: Qualified majority voting, based on the double-majority rule, is the main method used by the Council of the European Union to adopt EU legislation.
L30: 
L31: On this page
L32:

L34:   * 【28†When is a qualified majority reached?】
L35:   * 【29†Abstention】

L39: ## The most used voting method in the Council
L40: 
L41: Qualified majority is the voting system most frequently used in the Council, with about 80% of all EU legislation adopted through it.
L42: 
L43: This is because a qualified majority applies when the Council takes decisions under the ordinary legislative procedure, which is the primary decision-making process for adopting EU laws.
L44: 
L45: When the Council reaches a qualified majority, an EU legislative act is adopted.
L46: ## When is the qualified majority reached?
L47: 
L48: A qualified majority is reached if two conditions are simultaneously met:
L49: 
L50:   * at least 55% of member states vote in favour (15 out of 27)
L51:   * those member states represent at least 65% of the total EU population
L52: 
L53: This procedure is also known as the 'double-majority rule'.
L54: 
L55: 【33†Image】 55%
L56: 
L57: of the EU member states
L58: 
L59: 【34†Image】 65%
L60: 
L61: of the EU population
L62: ### Blocking minority
L63: 
L64: The blocking minority must include at least four member states. If there are fewer than four countries that vote against, the qualified majority is deemed attained.
L65: 
L66: For example, if all but three member states vote in favour of adopting a piece of legislation, the qualified majority is considered reached even if the 24 member states voting in favour represent less than 65% of the total EU population.
L67: In other words, when there are fewer than four Council members voting against, the population criterion becomes irrelevant for determining the qualified majority.
L68: ## Abstention
L69: 
L70: An abstention under qualified majority voting counts as a vote against, and therefore contributes to the (blocking) minority.
L71: 
L72: Abstention is not the same as not participating in the vote. Any member can abstain at any time.
L73: ## Reinforced qualified majority
L74: 
L75: The reinforced qualified majority system applies when the Council votes on a proposal which is not submitted by the European Commission or the High Representative of the European Union.
L76: 
L77: A reinforced qualified majority is reached if two conditions are simultaneously met:
L78: 
L79:   * at least 72% of member states vote in favour (at least 20 out of 27)
L80:   * member states supporting the proposal represent at least 65% of the EU population
L81: ## Special cases
L82: 
L83: In cases where not all member states participate in the vote, for example due to an opt-out in certain policy areas (e.g. euro, Schengen), specific voting rules apply. These  rules depend on the nature of the proposal.
L84: If the proposal comes from the Commission or the High Representative a decision is reached by qualified majority if 55% of the participating member states, representing at least 65% of the population of the participating member states, vote in favour. In this case, a blocking minority must include at least the minimum number of member states representing more than 35% of the EU population, plus one other member state.
L85: If the proposal does not come from the Commission or the High Representative, a reinforced qualified majority decision is adopted if 72% of the participating member states, representing at least 65% of the population of the participating member states, vote in favour.
L86: ## Voting calculator
L87: 
L88: The voting calculator helps find out whether the Council can reach one of the three voting thresholds required to adopt a legislative act.
L89: 
L90: Follow these four simple steps to check the final result of a Council vote:
L91: 
L92:   * choose a voting rule
L93:   * select the member states participating in the vote
L94:   * enter the votes
L95:   * verify the final result
